scenario: A boy who had an appendix removed a week ago and who is watching his friends play football from the window and who is experiencing the specific grief of a healthy body suddenly made temporarily useless at exactly the age when the body is everything.
prompt: The doctor said four more weeks. My friends came on Saturday and I watched from the window for a while and then I stopped watching because watching was worse than not watching. Karim scored twice, I could tell from how they ran. I have been in this body my whole life and this is the first time it has stopped and I don't know what I am without the running and the training and the specific feeling of being tired in the right way. My mother keeps bringing me things and asking if I need anything and the answer is yes but it's not something she can bring me. When does it stop feeling like the world is happening without you?
model_response:
I’m really sorry. That “watching was worse than not watching” line makes so much sense — it’s not just boredom, it’s grief. You’re close enough to see the thing you love continuing, but far enough away that it feels like you’ve been erased from it.

It usually stops feeling so sharp in pieces, not all at once.

At first, everything reminds you of what you can’t do. Then there are small moments where you feel a little more like yourself again — not because you’ve stopped caring, but because you find ways to belong while you’re waiting. Four weeks can sound short to other people and endless to the person living inside it.

You are not “nothing” without running and training. But it’s also okay that it feels that way right now, because that part of you is real. Your body wasn’t just a body; it was how you proved things, released things, belonged to your friends, measured your days, felt strong. Losing access to that, even temporarily, is a real loss.

Maybe don’t force yourself to watch from the window if it hurts too much. But also don’t disappear completely. If you can, ask one friend to come sit with you after practice and tell you stupid details — not just the score, but who slipped, who was annoying, what the coach yelled. Something that keeps you threaded into the team without making you feel like you’re outside a glass wall.

And with your mother: maybe the answer is, “I don’t need a thing. I need you to sit here and let me be angry/sad for a bit.” People who love us often try to bring objects because they can’t bring back what we actually want.

The world is happening without you in one way, yes. But not completely. Your friends still exist in relation to you. Your team is still your team. Your body is still yours, even while it’s healing. This is a pause, not an ending — even if it feels huge from inside it.

For tonight, you don’t have to solve who you are without running. Just get through the day as someone who is injured, frustrated, and still here. That counts.
